analysis.one_liner: Requires electronics makers to share repair parts, tools, and manuals with independent repair shops and owners.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or any floor action and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Repair Act would require companies that make digital electronics to sell repair documentation, parts, and tools to independent repair shops and device owners on the same terms they offer their own authorized shops. It bans "parts pairing" tricks that can disable a working replacement part or trigger false warnings after a repair. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce it. Car makers, dealers, and medical device makers are excluded.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of phones, laptops, appliances, farm equipment, and other electronics, who would be able to fix their own devices or use an independent shop without manufacturer restrictions. Independent repair businesses would gain access to parts, tools, and manuals that manufacturers currently hold back, letting them compete on equal footing with authorized repair providers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Device owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers must offer owners and independent repair providers the same documentation, parts, and tools they offer their own authorized repair providers, at the same prices and terms [S2].

The bill bans software "parts pairing" that prevents a functional replacement part from working, reduces device performance after a third-party repair, or displays false or non-dismissible warnings about non-manufacturer parts [S2].
If a device has a security lock, the manufacturer must still provide the special tools and documentation needed to disable and reset it during repair [S2].
The FTC would enforce violations as unfair or deceptive practices, and state attorneys general could sue on behalf of their residents for injunctions, penalties, and restitution [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Consumer electronics and other equipment manufacturers, who would lose control over repair pricing and the revenue they earn from monopoly parts and service, and would face enforcement costs. They argue they would also bear product liability and security risks, though the bill preserves trade-secret protections.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers and security researchers argue that opening repair tools and security-lock bypasses to independent shops can weaken device security and expose user data; the bill attempts to address this by keeping trade secrets confidential and limiting access to what repair requires [S2].

"Fair and reasonable terms" is defined relative to what an OEM gives its own authorized shops, which would likely require case-by-case FTC or court determinations and could make enforcement slow and contested [S2].
The bill does not cover cars, trucks, or medical devices, so it would not change repair restrictions in those large sectors [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real and direct: cheaper, faster repairs and longer device life for anyone who owns electronics, since owners would no longer be forced through manufacturer-controlled repair channels with paired parts and warning screens. The costs fall on manufacturers, who lose a profitable service monopoly, plus some plausible security and product-liability risk. The bill's narrow scope and its exclusion of cars and medical devices limit how much it could achieve, and its enforcement model relies on regulators comparing OEM terms shop by shop, which could be slow. On balance it is a consumer-friendly bill with a defined, modest scope.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced late in the session, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, and never reached a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph Morelle introduced the bill on May 23, 2024, for himself and Rep. Sara Perez, less than eight months before the 118th Congress adjourned [S2].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce, where no further action was recorded [S4].
Only four House members, all Democrats, signed on as cosponsors [S3].
The bill never received a committee vote, was never scheduled for floor consideration, and died when the 118th Congress ended [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electronics and equipment manufacturers are better off: they keep their control over repair parts, tools, and pricing, and device owners and independent repair shops continue to face the restrictions the bill would have removed. Committee leadership is better off in the sense that no member was forced to take a recorded position on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The House version drew only four cosponsors, all Democrats, so no meaningful partisan split on the bill itself is visible in the record; right-to-repair proposals generally draw support from both parties.

industries.note: The bill would force them to sell parts, tools, and manuals to independent shops at the same terms offered to their authorized providers, and bans parts-pairing software that disables non-manufacturer parts. This ends their control of repair pricing and service revenue, but would make repairs cheaper for the public.
Shops currently locked out of parts, tools, and diagnostic software would gain equal access and could compete with manufacturer-authorized providers.
The bill expressly excludes car makers, dealers, and vehicle equipment, leaving their existing restrictions on parts and repair in place.
The bill expressly excludes medical device makers, so hospitals and independent technicians cannot use it to force access to service materials.
